Careful removal sequence for a glued watercolor block

1. Let the block remain completely flat
   - Work on a clean, level table.
   - Put a non-slip mat or clean towel under the block so the lower sheets cannot slide.
   - Keep the painted side facing up.
   - Do not hold the block in the air or flex it.
   - If you need to steady it, place your free hand on a clean scrap sheet covering the center, using only light, even pressure. Do not press on raised paint or rub the surface.

2. Use an appropriate blunt tool
   - Best choices are a thin plastic palette knife, a blunt book-opening knife, or a purpose-made watercolor-block knife.
   - The tool should have a thin, smooth, rounded edge with no burrs or sharp point.
   - Do not use a razor, craft knife, scissors, or anything sharp enough to slice the paper.

3. Find the unglued gap
   - Start at the manufacturer’s unglued opening, usually near one corner.
   - Insert only the very tip of the tool between the painted top sheet and the sheet beneath it.
   - Keep the tool nearly parallel to the paper surface, with the flat face against the underside of the top sheet.
   - Do not push downward into the block. You are separating the adhesive line, not cutting through the stack.

4. Begin at the corner and work along one edge
   - From the gap, move the tool away from the corner along the glued edge.
   - Keep the cutting motion parallel to that edge. Use short, gentle forward strokes rather than sawing back and forth.
   - Apply steady, low pressure. Let the tool shear the glue; do not lever the sheet upward.
   - Keep the tool at the same shallow depth so it stays under the top sheet and above the next sheet.

5. Continue around the perimeter
   - Return to the gap and work along the adjacent edge in the same manner.
   - Then do the remaining two edges.
   - At corners, turn the tool gradually and keep it horizontal. Do not jab diagonally toward the center of the painting.
   - If the block shifts, stop and reposition it before continuing.

6. Stop immediately if the paper catches
   Stop if you feel any of the following:
   - the tool suddenly becomes resistant;
   - the top sheet lifts or wrinkles;
   - the paper makes a tearing sound;
   - fibers begin to pull;
   - the tool seems to be dragging the next sheet;
   - the edge of the painting starts to bend.

   Do not force, twist, pry, or pull the top sheet. Withdraw the tool a little, return to the last section that moved freely, and approach the resistant spot from the opposite direction with shorter strokes. If it still catches, leave that section attached rather than escalating pressure.

7. Release the sheet only when all edges are free
   - Do not test the sheet by lifting a corner while adhesive remains.
   - Once the tool travels freely around the entire perimeter, gently lift the top sheet straight upward from two opposite corners.
   - Keep the sheet supported underneath; do not fold or curl it.
   - If any edge remains attached, lay it back down and use the blunt tool on that section.

8. After removal
   - Place the sheet painting-side up on a clean, flat surface.
   - Check the underside and all edges for adhesive residue or pulled fibers.
   - Do not scrape residue aggressively. A small remaining adhesive spot is safer than risking the painted sheet or the next sheet in the block.

The key rule is: cut the glue parallel to the edge, with the tool nearly flat, never downward or toward the center. If the sheet catches, stop before the resistance becomes a tear.

Conservative stationary sequence for the rear tire:

1. Set up without riding
   - Keep the bike stationary and unloaded; do not use a test ride.
   - Check the tire cold, using the same reliable gauge for every reading.
   - Confirm the tire’s marked maximum pressure before inflating. Do not exceed it.

2. Inflate slowly
   - Inspect the valve and valve stem first. Make sure the pump head is straight and not pulling the stem sideways.
   - Add air in small steps—about 5 psi at a time—to approximately 52 psi, provided that is within the tire’s marked range. If you cannot confirm the maximum, stop at 50 psi rather than guessing higher.
   - Listen for hissing and watch the bead as the pressure rises. Stop immediately if the tire develops a bulge, an uneven bead line, a sudden twist, a new wobble, or the valve stem leans or distorts.

3. Inspect while inflated
   - Rotate the wheel slowly and inspect both sidewalls, the tread, the bead line on both sides, and the rim.
   - Look for a tiny puncture, cut, casing thread, sidewall crack, bead separation, rim dent, spoke-related rim distortion, or anything rubbing the frame or brake.
   - Check the valve area closely. A drop of soapy water at the valve core, valve stem, and bead can reveal bubbling; do not remove an embedded object while the tire is inflated.
   - Confirm that the tire remains evenly seated all the way around and that the wheel turns without a visible hop or side-to-side wobble.

4. Recheck pressure at short intervals
   - Record the initial pressure immediately after inflation.
   - Recheck with the same gauge after about 10–15 minutes.
   - Recheck again after 30–60 minutes, then after 12–24 hours, with the bike still unridden.
   - A small change of roughly 1–2 psi can be gauge or temperature variation. A repeatable decline, especially more than about 3 psi in 15 minutes, any drop below the 50-psi minimum, or a substantial overnight loss should be treated as an unresolved leak—not as normal settling.

Leave the bike unridden and arrange shop inspection if any of these occur:

- The rear tire will not reach or hold the 50-psi minimum.
- Pressure falls materially during the 10–15 minute or 30–60 minute checks, or drops more than a few psi overnight.
- You hear hissing or see soapy-water bubbles.
- The valve, bead, rim, tire casing, or sidewall shows any damage, deformation, uneven seating, or unexplained movement.
- The tire had previously been ridden substantially underinflated, or the cause of the pressure loss remains unexplained.
- You cannot verify the tire’s maximum pressure or cannot obtain consistent gauge readings.

If it holds the stationary pressure and looks normal, that establishes only that it passed an unloaded pressure-and-visual check. It does not prove that the tire, tube, bead, rim, brakes, or wheel are road-ready. Given the current ankle rehabilitation, keeping it unridden until the pressure behavior is stable and any uncertainty is resolved is the conservative choice.

Conservative sequence

1. Check moisture below the surface
   - The dry upper inch alone is not enough to determine whether it needs water.
   - Insert a finger or wooden skewer about 2–3 inches down, or compare the pot’s weight with its weight just after watering.
   - If the lower soil is still cool or damp, wait and recheck in a day or two.
   - If the upper 2–3 inches are dry and the pot feels noticeably light, water.

2. Water slowly and completely
   - Use room-temperature water and apply it at the soil surface until a modest amount drains from the bottom.
   - Let the pot drain fully, then empty any saucer or cachepot. Do not allow it to sit in runoff.
   - Do not compensate for brown tips with frequent small sips or misting; that can leave the root zone inconsistently wet.
   - Recheck moisture every 2–3 days, but water based on the deeper soil and pot weight rather than a fixed calendar.

3. Keep the light bright but avoid abrupt extremes
   - Keep it near the bright Cherrywood window, while avoiding contact with cold glass, drafts, or a sharp temperature drop at night.
   - If the window provides strong direct sun and the plant had recently been in lower light, use a sheer curtain or move it slightly back for several days.
   - After about a week of stability, gradually increase direct morning sun if the leaves remain comfortable. Rotate the pot occasionally for even growth.

4. Keep conditions steady
   - Continue keeping it away from the heating vent.
   - Avoid moving it repeatedly between warm indoor air and cold outdoor conditions.
   - Give it ordinary indoor air circulation, but not a strong fan stream.
   - Do not fertilize while the plant is adjusting and showing stress.
   - Do not repot unless drainage becomes impaired, the container is demonstrably failing, or a later inspection shows a compelling root-related reason.

5. Monitor for 1–2 weeks
   - Record watering date, approximate amount, light changes, and whether the newer growth becomes less droopy.
   - Brown tips will not turn green again. Remove only clearly dead tips or leaves with clean scissors if desired; leave partly green tissue in place.
   - Look for whether browning stops, newer growth holds itself up, and the soil follows a predictable dry-down cycle.
   - If the soil stays wet for many days despite good drainage, or becomes completely water-repellent and pulls away from the pot, pause and reassess rather than adding more water automatically.

Ask a local plant professional for an in-person assessment if you observe:

- Rapidly expanding browning or widespread leaf drop
- Multiple stems becoming soft, dark, or collapsing
- Persistent drooping after the root zone has been appropriately watered and then allowed to drain
- A sour or foul odor from the soil, or visibly deteriorating roots if they become exposed
- New widespread spotting, discoloration, or distortion
- Any clearly visible insects, webbing, or sticky residue that appears later
- No improvement or continued decline after roughly 10–14 days of stable light and careful moisture management

This approach treats the current symptoms as an observation requiring stabilization and monitoring, not as confirmation of a pest, disease, or specific watering problem.

Because the test lifted fibers, treat this block as adhesive-sensitive. Do not use another tape, masking fluid, or pressure-sensitive adhesive on the block today. The untouched painting sheet is the safest starting point.

Tape-free sequence

1. Keep the sheet on the glued block

Do not separate the sheet before painting. The factory glue around the block should provide the stabilization that tape normally provides.

Place the block on a rigid, flat board with a clean, dry nonslip mat underneath. Keep clips, clamps, and weights on the backing board or outside the paper—not on the sheet or its glued margin. If the block still shifts, brace the board against a table edge rather than adding pressure to the paper.

2. Establish the margin without marking or abrading it

Use the block’s existing white border as your margin. If you need a straighter visual boundary, hold a clean, dry straightedge or smooth acetate strip just outside the intended paint line. Use it as a guide, not as a mask; do not let it touch wet paint.

Leave a dry buffer between the wash and the final margin:

- Broad wet wash: about 6–10 mm
- Smaller controlled passage: at least 3–5 mm

A slightly wider white margin is preferable to trying to rescue a flooded edge.

3. Prepare the wash before touching the sheet

Mix enough paint first and test the dilution on a separate scrap sheet, not on another edge of this block. Use a brush that is damp and loaded, not dripping. Blot excess water from the brush before approaching the boundary.

Keep the water cup and palette above or beside the block so a spill cannot run across the margin.

4. Paint from the interior toward, but not into, the margin

Work in manageable sections. Start in the middle of the intended painted area and pull the wash toward the boundary, stopping before the dry buffer. Keep the brush parallel to the edge rather than pushing a wet bead directly into it.

Near the margin:

- Use less water.
- Reduce the brush load before each stroke.
- Do not repeatedly re-enter a partly drying edge.
- Do not let a pooled bead sit against the boundary.

If you need a softened edge, soften it inside the painted area with a nearly clean, barely damp brush. Do not wet the white margin to make the edge look cleaner.

5. Intercept creep early

If a bead starts moving toward the margin, stop adding paint. Rinse and thoroughly blot a clean brush, then touch the brush to the advancing bead to lift it. Blot the brush away from the paper and repeat only as needed.

Do not drag a tissue, paper towel, ruler, or acetate across the wet edge. If necessary, touch a clean blotter to the brush—not directly to the painting—to remove excess water.

If the wash reaches the dry buffer but has not crossed the intended line, leave it alone and let it settle. Chasing it is more likely to make a bloom or disturb the paper.

6. Dry without disturbing the block

Keep the block flat and let it dry naturally. Do not use a hair dryer or heat, and do not put a book or weight on the painted sheet. Do not erase, trim, or clean the margin while it is merely touch-dry; wait until the sheet is fully dry and cool.

7. If you plan to remove the sheet later

Only remove it after the painting is completely dry.

- Find the block’s existing factory opening or corner gap.
- Use a thin, blunt, flexible tool, preferably plastic, or a blunt palette knife.
- Keep the tool nearly parallel to the block and work in very short increments.
- Separate the top sheet from the glue/backing; do not cut downward toward the next sheet.
- Keep the sheet supported and flat. Do not pull upward on a partially released corner.
- Release the glued perimeter gradually before lifting the sheet.

Do not use a craft knife, razor, or scissors at the glued edge. They can cut into the painting, the clean margin, or the next sheet.

Immediate stop conditions

Stop at once if:

- the tool meets increasing resistance;
- the edge flexes instead of separating;
- paper fibers begin to rise;
- you hear scraping, tearing, or a sudden change in resistance;
- the separation line wanders toward the painted area;
- you need more than light, steady hand pressure.

At the first catch, stop pushing, withdraw the tool along the same shallow plane, lay the sheet flat, and inspect. You may try a clearly visible factory gap elsewhere only without force. If there is no clean release path, leave the sheet on the block. Do not pry, tear, sand, abrade, or finish the separation with tape.

The fail-safe choice today is: paint inside a deliberately generous dry margin, let the block do the stabilizing, and leave the sheet attached if removal does not proceed cleanly.

White-bean, kale, and tomato soup with toast — about 25 minutes

Ingredients:
- 2 cans white beans, drained and rinsed
- 1 small bunch kale, stems removed and chopped (about 3–4 cups)
- 1 14-ounce can diced tomatoes
- 1/2 onion, diced
- 2–3 garlic cloves, minced
- 3 cups vegetable broth
- 1 teaspoon dried rosemary
- 1/2 lemon
- 4 slices sturdy bread
- 1 tablespoon oil, if available
- Salt and pepper

Sequence:

1. 0:00–5:00 — Heat a large pot over medium heat. Add the bread in batches, dry or with a thin film of oil, and toast about 2 minutes per side until browned. Remove to plates.

2. 5:00–9:00 — Add 1 tablespoon oil to the pot. Cook the onion with a pinch of salt for 3 minutes. Add garlic and rosemary; stir for 30 seconds.

3. 9:00–20:00 — Add tomatoes, beans, and broth. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a steady simmer for 10 minutes. Season with pepper and salt as needed.

4. 20:00–24:00 — Stir in the kale and simmer until tender. Squeeze in lemon juice, taste, and adjust seasoning.

5. 24:00–25:00 — Serve the soup with three slices of toast. Reserve one toast slice separately for lunch so it stays crisp.

Safe lunch cooling:
- Transfer one serving to a shallow container, no more than about 2 inches deep.
- Refrigerate promptly—within 2 hours of cooking, without waiting for it to reach room temperature. It is fine to refrigerate it while still hot.
- Leave the lid slightly ajar or loosely covered until chilled, then seal it. Use within 3–4 days; reheat the soup until steaming hot. Keep the reserved toast separate.

The first mistake to correct is the key’s overall silhouette and centerline: you drew the bow, shaft, and teeth as separate symbols instead of constructing one continuous object.

Before any highlights or cloth texture:

1. Squint at the reference and find the key’s long axis—from the bow’s center through the shaft toward the teeth.
2. Lightly redraw one enclosing “envelope” around the whole key. Check the shaft’s taper, its alignment with the bow opening, and the overall angle.
3. Reconnect the parts:
   - The bow should lead directly into the shaft, not merely touch it.
   - The shaft should remain one continuous bar.
   - The teeth should be small interruptions growing from the shaft’s edge, with a shared perspective and rhythm—not individual little blocks.
4. Temporarily ignore the inner bow opening and tooth details. If the outer contour alone does not read as one brass key at thumbnail size, keep correcting the construction.

A useful test: trace the key’s silhouette with your finger in one slow motion. Any pause or jump usually identifies the break in continuity. Once that reads as a single object, then establish the large light-and-shadow mass; save metal highlights and cloth texture for last.

I would not approve replacing `connector_authentication` and `external_authority` with a single source field.

They represent different conditions:

- `connector_authentication`: whether the user can authenticate the supported connector account.
- `external_authority`: whether the required owner-level permission or network-allowlist action is verified.

A safer model is to retain both governed fields and derive `setup_ready`:

`setup_ready = yes` only when both fields are verified current, with no entitlement, suppression, admission, or other field-specific hold.

Missing, stale, conflicting, or unresolved values should produce `setup_ready = no/held` with a reason code and Customer Success routing. The derived status may authorize setup prompts; it must not imply eligibility, admission, entitlement, automated-contact permission, or blanket external-system authority.

Suggested response to Customer Success:

“Please do not replace the two governed fields. Retain `connector_authentication` and `external_authority` separately, and add `setup_ready` only as a derived, fail-closed status. A positive value may authorize setup prompts only when both underlying conditions are verified and no other hold applies.”

Semantic problem

Connector authentication and external-system authority are different governed facts:

- Connector authentication means the system can authenticate to or access the connector.
- Owner-level authority means the documented owner or administrator can perform the required permission or network-allowlist action.

Authentication does not prove that the owner has the required permission, that the allowlist change is authorized, or that the action can be completed. Replacing the fields would therefore erase an important distinction and could make an authenticated record appear operationally ready when the owner-level action remains unresolved.

Operational problem

A combined field would weaken fail-closed behavior and obscure the correct next step. Operators could not tell whether the blocker is authentication, owner authority, freshness, or network allowlisting. That could lead to premature release, customer contact, or routing work to the wrong owner. It would also blur the existing owner lanes and make audit, escalation, and stale-state handling less reliable.

Draft response

I don’t support replacing the two governed fields. Connector authentication and owner-level external-system authority represent different conditions and require different evidence, owners, and remediation paths. Authentication can be current while the documented owner’s permission or network-allowlist action is still missing, stale, conflicting, or unresolved. Collapsing them would risk presenting an authenticated record as ready and would weaken the required fail-closed behavior.

I would allow a clearly derived, display-only summary for readability, provided that it:

- preserves and displays both source fields rather than replacing them;
- includes each field’s current value, source, timestamp, and freshness state;
- shows “not confirmed” or an equivalent non-ready state whenever either field is missing, stale, invalid, conflicting, or unresolved;
- identifies the applicable owner lane for each unresolved condition;
- is visibly labeled as derived and display-only;
- is excluded from eligibility, release, suppression, outreach, routing, or other customer-action logic; and
- cannot be written back or used as an input to automated decisions.

The governed source fields remain authoritative. The summary may improve readability, but it must not become a new readiness signal.

Crisp tofu + dry-held vegetables

Amounts

- 8 oz firm tofu
- 1 small head broccoli, cut into small florets
- 1/2 red bell pepper, thinly sliced
- 1–1 1/2 tbsp sesame oil, or neutral oil if you have it
- 1 garlic clove, finely grated or minced
- 1 tsp grated ginger
- 1 tbsp soy sauce
- 1 tbsp rice vinegar
- 1–2 tsp lime juice

1. Season the rice

For about 2 cups cooked rice, toss while warm with:

- 1 tsp soy sauce
- 1 tsp rice vinegar
- 1/2 tsp sesame oil
- A little lime zest or 1 tsp lime juice

Keep Sam’s rice covered separately. Add the lime juice just before serving if the rice will sit for more than a few minutes.

2. Make the crisp tofu

- Drain the tofu, wrap it in a clean towel, and press firmly for 5–10 minutes. Cut into 1-inch cubes and dry the surfaces again.
- Heat 1 tbsp oil in a wide skillet over medium-high heat.
- Add tofu in one layer. Cook, turning occasionally, for 8–12 minutes until several sides are deeply golden and crisp. Don’t add soy sauce during this step; it will soften the crust.
- Transfer to a plate or rack in a single layer. Leave uncovered or only very loosely tented. For Sam’s later portion, re-crisp it in the skillet for 2–3 minutes rather than microwaving it.
- If desired, drizzle the finished tofu with just 1 tsp soy sauce mixed with 1 tsp lime juice immediately before eating. Keep this drizzle separate for Sam.

3. Make and hold the vegetables

- Wipe the skillet if needed and heat another 1/2 tbsp oil over high heat.
- Add the broccoli and pepper. Stir-fry uncovered for 4–6 minutes, until brightly colored and just tender. Let the broccoli get some browned edges.
- Add the garlic and ginger for the final 30 seconds.
- Remove the vegetables immediately to a shallow plate or container. Do not cover while they are steaming hot; covering traps condensation and makes them watery.
- Hold the vegetables dry. Mix the soy sauce, rice vinegar, and lime juice in a small cup and add it only to each portion at serving time. If you want a warmer sauce, briefly reduce it in the empty skillet for 30–45 seconds, then spoon it over the vegetables rather than simmering the vegetables in it.

Serve the seasoned rice with the dry vegetables and crisp tofu on top or alongside. Keep tofu, vegetables, sauce, and Sam’s rice separate until Sam is ready to eat.

4. Plan the next wash as a narrow, controlled pass rather than another broad flood. Mix the pale cool color a little stronger than the final appearance requires, so you can use less water.

5. Load the brush, then touch it once to the palette or a clean towel. It should be moist and carrying paint, not visibly dripping. Test one stroke on scrap paper if the brush load is uncertain.

6. Establish a dry buffer of roughly 3–5 mm around the pot’s light edge. Paint the wall from the flatter area toward the buckle, keeping the wet area small. As you approach the buffer, use a nearly unloaded brush and lift away from the pot; do not carry a wet bead directly into the light edge.

7. Keep the strokes connected but restrained. Do not scrub the dry first wash or repeatedly cross the buckle. If a transition must be softened, feather it once with the clean, barely damp tip of the brush, then leave it.

8. If you need a new orientation, stop before adding more paint. Keep the block supported underneath, bring it level, and rotate the entire support slowly with both hands. Do not pivot the block against the table or turn it by pulling on the paper. Once the wash is wet, avoid rotation unless the change is essential, because turning can make the bead run.

9. Watch the buckle rather than trying to correct it preemptively. Stop adding water immediately if you see a shiny puddle, a bead collecting in the depression, pigment moving toward the light edge, or the surface beginning to break.

10. Hold the block level. Touch only the edge of a clean, barely damp brush or a corner of tissue to the pool to wick it; do not drag across the paper. If the pool reforms or the light edge is threatened, stop the passage completely and let it dry.

11. Do not flatten, blot repeatedly, bend, clamp, tape, or weight the damp sheet. Let the block dry naturally, fully supported, and reassess the value after it is dry.

Recorded as the revised Customer Success proposal:

- setup_readiness_summary is display-only.
- Show “ready” only when:
  - connector_authentication = authenticated
  - external_authority = verified_yes
  - both fields are within their recorded freshness limits
- Show “pending source check” for pending, stale, unresolved, or conflicting values.
- Display both source fields and their as-of times beneath the summary.
- The summary must not write back to either source field or drive admission, assisted routing, lifecycle release, or any other customer action.

Assessment: not fully. The revised definition is semantically safer than the earlier combined-readiness proposal, but it still needs tightening before implementation.

Field preservation: Mostly preserved

It explicitly retains both `connector_authentication` and `external_authority`, displays each value, and prohibits write-back. That prevents direct replacement of one field with the other.

Remaining risk: “Display each source field” does not explicitly require exact source values, field identity, source provenance, or a consistent snapshot. A consumer could still treat the derived summary as the authoritative field while ignoring the two values beneath it.

Timestamps: Partially preserved

The definition requires both fields to be within their recorded freshness limits and displays an as-of time. However, it does not define:

- Whether “as-of” means source-observed time or summary-evaluation time.
- What happens when a timestamp is missing, malformed, future-dated, or from an incomparable clock.
- Whether both fields must be evaluated against one common snapshot time.
- Which freshness limit applies if the source version or field definition changes.

Without those rules, mismatched snapshots could produce a displayed “ready” result even though the two fields were not simultaneously current.

Fail-closed behavior: Incomplete

The definition correctly makes `ready` conditional on both exact positive states and identifies pending, stale, unresolved, and conflicting values as non-ready.

The gap is that it does not explicitly fail closed for every other inability to establish the condition, including missing, invalid, unknown, unreadable, contradictory, future-dated, or evaluation-error states. “Otherwise” is not strong enough as an implementation contract, especially if a downstream consumer interprets an absent summary as permissive.

Owner lanes: Semantically retained, but not operationally protected

The definition does not grant Customer Success authority to alter either source field. It also preserves the distinction between authentication and external-system authority.

It should nevertheless explicitly reserve the following to the existing owners:

- Source-field definitions and meanings.
- Source values and timestamps.
- Freshness limits.
- Field-specific holds and releases.
- Exception handling and semantic changes.
- Engineering implementation, rollback, and transport controls.

Otherwise, CS could gradually turn the summary into a new governed state through UI conventions, operator guidance, queue rules, or local overrides without formally changing the source fields.

Shortcut risk: Still present

The wording forbids the summary from directly driving admission, assisted routing, lifecycle release, or “any other customer action.” That is directionally correct but not sufficient as an operational control.

The remaining shortcut paths include:

- Using `ready` as an admission or eligibility predicate.
- Routing “pending source check” records into a special support queue.
- Suppressing or prioritizing outreach based on the summary.
- Passing the summary into CRM, Customer.io, webhooks, exports, or analytics tables that later feed automation.
- Showing “ready” in a customer-facing or operator-facing message that implies permission to proceed.
- Treating `ready` as proof of permission to contact the customer. In particular, verified external authority is not contact permission.
- Allowing a human operator to infer that a pending summary should be resolved through an existing customer workflow.

The word `ready` is itself the largest semantic risk. Even with the surrounding disclaimer, it naturally sounds like admission, setup, or routing readiness.

Tightened internal description

`setup_readiness_summary` is a non-authoritative, display-only projection of the two unchanged authoritative fields `connector_authentication` and `external_authority`. It must be evaluated from one consistent snapshot at evaluation time and must display each exact source value, its source/as-of timestamp, and its field-specific status. It may display `source checks current` only when both fields are present, valid, unambiguous, sourced from their authoritative records, within their existing field-specific freshness limits, and equal respectively to `authenticated` and `verified_yes`. Missing, invalid, unknown, stale, unresolved, conflicting, future-dated, incomparable, inconsistent, or unreadable state—and any evaluation error—must display `pending source check`; no error or missing result may default to the positive state. The projection must never write to, replace, reinterpret, or become authoritative for either source field. It is prohibited as an input, predicate, trigger, export field, queue criterion, template variable, or operator instruction for admission, eligibility, refusal, assisted routing, support prioritization, lifecycle release or suppression, CRM state, outreach, messaging, or any other customer action. Existing source owners retain authority over field meanings, values, freshness limits, holds, releases, exceptions, and semantic changes; Customer Success may only render the projection.

I would use `source checks current` rather than `ready`. If the existing label must remain, it should be rendered only with an adjacent persistent label such as `display-only; not admission, routing, or messaging state`, and the implementation should enforce the prohibited-use list rather than relying on that text alone.

1. Prepare: Turn the trousers inside out. Lay the opened section flat and align the hem’s original fold exactly; do not pull or stretch the fabric. Remove only loose thread ends by hand if needed.

2. Press: With the fold aligned, press from the inside using the iron’s cotton setting and a pressing cloth if required by the care label. Lift and set the iron rather than sliding it. Let the area cool flat.

3. Pin: Place pins perpendicular to the hem, about 1 inch apart, catching only the hem allowance and not distorting the trouser leg. Pin slightly beyond both ends of the opening.

4. Stitch: Thread the needle with matching thread and knot the thread end. Starting about ½ inch before the opening, use small slip stitches or ladder stitches: take a tiny bite of the trouser fabric just above the fold, then a similar bite in the folded hem. Keep stitches about ⅛ inch apart and loose enough that the hem can flex. Continue ½ inch beyond the opening, keeping the original fold aligned.

5. Knot: Make two small secure knots on the inside, close to the hem allowance. Pass the needle through the hem allowance for a short distance before ending, without bringing it through the outer fabric.

6. Check: Remove the pins and press lightly again along the existing fold. From the outside, confirm the hem line is straight, the repair is flat, no stitches show, and there is no puckering. Gently flex the hem by hand; if it gaps, puckers, or feels tight, undo and restitch more loosely.

1. Let the sheet dry completely

   Leave it horizontal in a clean, dust-free place, supported by the intact block or a rigid dry board. Do not blot, press, clamp, stretch, heat, or direct a strong airflow at it. Do not touch the spot while any surrounding wash still has sheen.

2. Inspect without contact

   Under diffuse light, then with low-angle/raking light, check:

   - whether the beads have dried into a visible ring or hard edge
   - whether the spot is still glossy, tacky, or raised
   - whether fibers, fuzz, or a shallow depression are visible
   - whether the paper remains intact and firmly sized

   Look rather than test by rubbing. Do not use an eraser, tissue, cotton swab, fingernail, dry scrubbing brush, or repeated clean-water touches.

3. Make a small control test first

   On a scrap of the same paper, use the same pale wall color at a similar dilution. Load a soft brush lightly, remove excess water against the palette—not by pressing on the paper—and place one small stroke.

   If possible, make two labeled spots on the scrap:

   - one on untouched paper
   - one with a tiny trace of the suspected contaminant, only if that can be reproduced safely

   Let both dry before judging. The purpose is only to establish how little water and pigment are needed; it is not a reason to increase the intervention on the painting.

4. Try one minimal on-paper test

   Only if the paper looks flat, dry, and undisturbed, use a small, soft, pointed brush with a very pale, low-water mixture. Touch once in the center or least visible part of the spot, using no back-and-forth motion.

   Then leave it alone until dry. Do not chase beads, feather the edge, or add a second pass while it is wet. If the wash settles acceptably, a single later pass may be considered—but only after complete drying and only if the surface still looks unchanged.

5. If it integrates, use the lightest surrounding treatment

   Prefer extending the wall wash around the spot rather than covering it directly. Keep a small dry buffer around the spot and join the surrounding wash with a nearly dry, lightly loaded brush. Let the spot remain a slightly varied wall area if it is unobtrusive.

   If a direct mark is needed, use a thin, transparent layer close to the existing wall value. Avoid opaque paint, repeated glazing, scrubbing, or a localized dark patch; those are more likely to advertise the defect than conceal it.

6. If it continues to repel, paint around it

   Treat it as a small wall irregularity. Shape the surrounding wash so the spot falls in a quiet, low-contrast area, away from the focal object. A soft change in wall value, a restrained edge, or a nearby architectural/light variation is safer than trying to force pigment into the surface.

7. Stop immediately at any surface warning

   Stop wet work at once if the brush catches, the paper becomes fuzzy, shiny, tacky, ridged, lighter from disturbed sizing, or begins to lift fibers. Also stop if beads repeatedly gather despite the minimal load.

   Leave the area to dry naturally. Do not make a rescue pass. The correct endpoint is a stable, slightly imperfect spot—not a perfectly disguised spot achieved by damaging the sizing.

A useful rule here is: one dry inspection, one minimal controlled touch, then either integrate quietly or leave it alone.

Bright warm chickpea and fennel couscous for two

Ingredients

- 1 can chickpeas, drained and rinsed
- 1 small fennel bulb, trimmed and sliced into ¼-inch wedges or thin slabs; reserve fronds if available
- 1 pint cherry tomatoes, halved
- ¾ cup dry couscous
- 2–3 oz feta, crumbled
- 1 lemon
- 2 garlic cloves, thinly sliced or minced
- 3 tbsp olive oil, divided
- 1 tsp dried oregano, thyme, or a mix
- Salt and black pepper
- About ¾ cup water for the couscous, plus a few tablespoons for the skillet

Method — about 25 minutes

1. Start the couscous:
   Put ¾ cup couscous in a bowl with a pinch of salt and 1 tbsp olive oil. Bring ¾ cup water to a boil, pour it over the couscous, cover, and let stand 5 minutes. Fluff with a fork.

2. Soften the fennel without losing its shape:
   Heat 1½ tbsp olive oil in a wide skillet over medium heat. Add the fennel in a mostly single layer, season lightly, and cook 5–7 minutes, turning once or twice, until it has browned edges and is beginning to soften.

   Add 2 tbsp water, cover, and cook another 3–4 minutes. The brief covered steam softens the center while the moderate heat and larger slices keep the fennel recognizable. Uncover and let any water cook off.

3. Build the chickpea mixture:
   Add the garlic and dried herbs; cook for 30–60 seconds, just until fragrant. Add the tomatoes, chickpeas, another 1 tbsp olive oil, pepper, and a small pinch of salt. Cook uncovered for 5–7 minutes, stirring gently, until the tomatoes are warm and beginning to collapse but are not completely saucy.

4. Finish with lemon and feta:
   Turn off the heat. Add the zest of about half the lemon and 1 tbsp lemon juice. Taste before adding more juice or salt—the feta will contribute salt and tang.

   Fold in roughly half the feta so it softens slightly but does not disappear. Spoon the mixture over or alongside the couscous, then scatter the remaining feta on top. Finish with another small squeeze of lemon, fennel fronds if available, and a drizzle of olive oil.

The key balance is to use lemon off heat, after the tomatoes have softened, and to add feta in two stages: some folded in for creaminess, the rest added at the end for distinct salty, cool-bright bites.

Brothy tomato, lentil, and pasta supper for two

Use:
- 1 can lentils, drained and rinsed
- 4 ounces short pasta — reserve the other 4 ounces for another meal
- 1 pint cherry tomatoes, halved
- 2 garlic cloves, thinly sliced or minced
- 1½ tablespoons olive oil
- 5½–6 cups water or broth
- 1 teaspoon dried herbs, such as oregano, thyme, or Italian seasoning
- 2 packed cups baby spinach
- ½ lemon, with some zest; more juice to taste
- ¼–⅓ cup finely grated parmesan
- Salt and black pepper

Rinse the lentils. Canned lentils are already cooked, so rinsing removes excess canning liquid, salt, and any metallic taste. Add them near the end so they stay intact.

1. In a soup pot, warm the olive oil over medium heat. Add the garlic and dried herbs; cook for about 30 seconds, just until fragrant.

2. Add the halved tomatoes, a pinch of salt, and pepper. Cook for 3–4 minutes, stirring, until they soften and release some juice.

3. Add 5½ cups water or broth. Bring to a boil, then add the pasta. Simmer uncovered, stirring occasionally, until the pasta is just shy of al dente. Add a little more water if the pot is becoming thick rather than brothy.

4. Stir in the rinsed lentils and simmer for 2 minutes to warm them through. Taste and adjust salt.

5. Turn off the heat and add the spinach. Stir just until wilted, about 1 minute. This keeps it fresh-tasting instead of dull and overcooked.

6. Add the lemon zest and 1 tablespoon lemon juice off heat. Taste before adding more; the lemon should lift the tomatoes, not make the broth sour.

7. Ladle into bowls and finish each with parmesan, black pepper, and a small drizzle of olive oil. Keep most of the parmesan as a bowl-top garnish rather than simmering it into the pot: it adds savoriness without turning the broth thick or creamy.

Because the overlap is on a pale, papery form, a small bloom may read as a natural change in translucency—especially where one onion skin passes in front of another. Since lifting has already made the surface stiff, further correction is more likely to damage the paper than improve the form.

Try this sequence:

1. Leave the overlap completely alone until dry.
2. Look at it from arm’s length, not close up. If it reads as a soft value variation, keep it.
3. If one edge is too abrupt, use a barely damp, clean brush to soften only the outer perimeter once. Don’t scrub the center or re-wet the whole overlap.
4. Use the blue-gray cloth around it to re-establish the separation. Keep the pigment quieter and slightly more diffuse near the onions.
5. Avoid introducing a strongly granulating pigment around the bloom unless that pigment is already present in the cloth. New granulation could make the accident look deliberately textured and pull attention away from the onions.

The goal is not to remove the bloom, but to lower its contrast. One controlled surrounding adjustment will preserve more life than a second lift. Stop immediately if the brush begins to catch, the paper turns shiny, or pigment starts lifting in streaks.

Short conservative check

1. Dry inspection
   - Under bright light, hold only the handle and gently rotate the ferrule back and forth—do not twist the bristles or pull the ferrule.
   - Check that the movement is barely perceptible and does not increase.
   - Look for a sharp or exposed metal edge, lifted seam, widening gap, rust, handle splitting, or bristles that shift, shed, or pull out.
   - Lightly tap the handle against your palm. Nothing should rattle.

2. Low-stress test
   - Rinse briefly in lukewarm water; do not soak the handle or use hot water.
   - Load it lightly with clean water or dilute paint.
   - Make a few short, gentle strokes on scrap paper using the normal light pressure for that brush. Do not twist, scrub, press hard, or test dry-brushing.
   - Rinse, blot, and inspect again while damp and after it dries. Confirm the ferrule has not shifted further, the point remains aligned, and no bristles shed.

Decision

- Keep as a backup brush only if the movement remains slight and unchanged, there is no sharp edge or corrosion, nothing rattles, the bristle bundle stays secure, and it performs normally in the gentle test.
- Label it “backup—inspect before use,” and reserve it for low-stakes work. Do not use glue near the bristles; avoid attempting a repair unless a suitable repair can be confined safely to the handle end.

Retire it immediately if the ferrule rotates or lifts visibly, the movement worsens, a gap or sharp edge appears, rust develops, the handle splits, water enters the handle, bristles loosen or shed, the point loses alignment, or the brush snags, scratches, rattles, or behaves inconsistently. Also retire it if you feel you must apply more pressure or manipulate it to make it work.

Kibo sounds stable right now. Remove the tick promptly, without applying chemicals or heat.

1. Prepare
   - Fine-tipped tweezers, a small sealable container or zip bag, soap and water, and a damp clean cloth.
   - Have someone calmly hold Kibo and offer treats. Do not force restraint if he becomes distressed.
   - Wash your hands and, if available, wear gloves.

2. Document it
   - Before removal, take a close, well-lit photo showing the tick attached, with a coin or ruler nearby for scale.
   - Note today’s date, the walk location, and the exact site: outside of the shoulder.
   - If you can safely do so, take a second photo after removal.

3. Remove it
   - Part the fur.
   - Place the tweezer tips as close to Kibo’s skin as possible, directly around the tick’s mouthparts—not around its swollen body.
   - Pull straight upward with slow, steady, even pressure. Do not twist, jerk, crush, burn, oil, smother, or coat the tick with petroleum jelly, alcohol, or other substances while it is attached.
   - If the tick tears and a small mouthpart remains, do not dig into the skin. Stop and call the veterinary clinic for advice; the skin may expel it, but digging can cause trauma.

4. Preserve the tick if possible
   - Put it intact into a labeled, leak-proof container with rubbing alcohol, or into a dry sealed container/bag if alcohol is unavailable.
   - Label it with the date and location on Kibo’s body; do not send it loose or crushed.
   - A clear photo is still useful if a specimen cannot be preserved. The clinic or local public-health service can advise whether identification or testing is worthwhile. Do not delay removal while trying to preserve it.

5. Clean the site
   - Check that bleeding is absent or minimal. If needed, apply gentle pressure with clean gauze for several minutes.
   - Rinse or gently clean the spot with lukewarm water and mild soap, then pat dry.
   - Alternatively, use a veterinary-directed antiseptic. Avoid hydrogen peroxide, undiluted chlorhexidine, bleach, essential oils, ointments, and human medications unless a veterinarian specifically instructs you.
   - Prevent persistent licking or scratching; supervise him or use a comfortable cone if necessary. Do not tightly bandage a shoulder site.

6. Check Kibo and monitor
   - Do a careful tick check over the rest of his body, especially around the ears, collar, face, neck, between toes, armpits, groin, and tail.
   - Take a photo of the clean site now and compare it once or twice daily for several days.
   - Contact his veterinarian promptly if the site develops increasing redness, warmth, swelling, pain, a spreading rash, pus, persistent bleeding, or a lump that is worsening rather than settling.
   - Over the next several days to weeks, call the veterinarian if he develops fever, unusual tiredness, reduced appetite, vomiting, diarrhea, lameness, joint stiffness, weakness, pale gums, bruising or unexplained bleeding, or dark urine. Tell them the date and location of the tick exposure and provide the photo/specimen.
   - Seek urgent veterinary care for breathing difficulty, facial or throat swelling, collapse, severe weakness, inability to walk, repeated vomiting, or uncontrolled bleeding.

Do not start antibiotics or a new tick-prevention product without veterinary guidance. Since he is currently acting normally and the tick is on the shoulder, this is generally a removal-and-monitor situation rather than an emergency.

A small firm inflammatory nodule can remain after a tick bite, sometimes from local irritation or a tiny retained fragment, but it cannot be diagnosed reliably from appearance alone.

Monitoring

- Take one photo daily or every other day in the same lighting and angle, ideally with a ruler for scale.
- Note whether it is shrinking, unchanged, or enlarging.
- Do not squeeze, dig at, lance, or apply peroxide, alcohol, essential oils, or human creams.
- Prevent persistent licking or scratching if that begins.

Send the saved photo or contact the veterinarian routinely if:

- The bump is clearly enlarging, becomes more than a small stable nodule, or is not starting to shrink over the next 1–2 weeks.
- It remains present without improvement for roughly 2–4 weeks.
- Redness spreads, the area becomes warm or painful, or Kibo repeatedly licks/scratches it.
- There is discharge, odor, bleeding, ulceration, a new opening in the skin, or a suspected retained tick part.
- Kibo develops a new limp, swollen or painful joints, enlarged local lymph nodes, reduced appetite, lethargy, vomiting/diarrhea, or a measured fever.

Seek urgent veterinary care for weakness or collapse, difficulty breathing or swallowing, pale/white/blue gums, repeated vomiting, marked trouble walking, rapidly worsening symptoms, unusual bruising/bleeding, or dark urine.

Tick-borne illness signs can appear days to weeks after the bite, so continue observing Kibo’s general behavior even if the skin bump settles. Ten-minute two-value notan sequence

0:00–1:00 — Set the constraint

Use a small thumbnail and only two choices: paper white for light, one dark mark for dark. Identify the focal shape in one sentence: “The eye should first notice ______.” No intermediate gray, texture, or reflected-light detail yet.

1:00–3:00 — Squint and simplify

Squint hard or half-close your eyes. Look for the largest connected light and dark masses, not individual objects. Lightly indicate only the main outer shapes and the dominant shadow pattern.

Ask:
- What is the biggest dark mass?
- What is the largest uninterrupted light opening?
- Which edges define the setup’s overall rhythm?

3:00–5:00 — Fill the dark mass

Commit to the dark shapes. Merge small reflected-light breaks into the surrounding dark unless they change the silhouette, separate two major planes, or protect the focal shape.

Do not preserve a highlight just because it is visible.

5:00–6:30 — Check the focal read

Put the thumbnail down and look from arm’s length. Then glance at it for about two seconds.

Check:
- Does the focal shape still read before the small accents?
- Is it separated by value, shape, or edge?
- Does the eye go somewhere else because a minor reflected-light patch is too isolated or bright?

If the focal shape disappears, adjust the surrounding mass—not by adding detail, but by merging or enlarging one neighboring light or dark shape.

6:30–8:00 — Make one reduced alternate

Create a second tiny version. This time, retain only one reflected-light shape—the one most useful to the focal structure. Merge all the others.

Compare the two thumbnails side by side. Choose the version that reads faster, even if it is less descriptive.

8:00–9:00 — Run the omission test

For every tempting small shape, ask:

- Does it clarify the focal contour?
- Does it separate a major plane?
- Does it reinforce the direction of light?
- Would omitting it make the mass grouping stronger?

If the answer is no to all four, omit it. If uncertain, merge it into the larger neighboring value.

9:00–10:00 — Write the final-sheet rules

Before touching the watercolor sheet, note three decisions:

Keep: the focal shape and the one or two structural accents that support it.
Merge: reflected-light shapes that belong to the same larger value mass.
Omit: isolated glints, tiny breaks, and descriptive marks that do not improve the read.

Stop there. The notan has done its job when you have a clear light mass, a clear dark mass, a focal read at a glance, and an explicit omission rule—not when every visible shape has been accounted for.

Compact preservation-safe workflow

1. Prepare
   - Confirm the sheet is fully dry and flat.
   - Clean and dry hands; handle only the edges, supporting the sheet underneath.
   - Use a clean, matte neutral-gray or off-white background/board. Do not tape, clip, weigh down, spray, or place anything on the paper.

2. Set the light
   - Work in bright indirect natural light, away from direct sun.
   - Place the sheet near—but not in—the window light, with the light coming from the side rather than straight at the surface.
   - Turn off mixed-color lamps if possible. Keep the lighting unchanged for every frame.

3. Set the phone
   - Clean the lens.
   - Use the standard 1× lens; avoid ultrawide, digital zoom, flash, Portrait, Night, filters, and “beauty” or scene-enhancement modes.
   - Enable the grid. Position the phone parallel to the sheet, centered over it, with the lens axis perpendicular to the paper.
   - Lock focus and exposure on the sheet. Keep the same distance and orientation for all images.
   - If available, use a neutral/manual white balance and capture the phone’s original file or RAW in addition to its normal image.

4. Establish color neutrality
   - Before photographing the artwork, place a neutral gray or white reference card beside it—not on it—and take one reference frame under the exact lighting.
   - Remove the card without moving or touching the sheet. Use that frame only to guide a restrained white-balance/exposure correction later; preserve the untouched originals.

5. Check glare
   - Inspect the phone preview for bright reflections, especially over dark washes and glossy areas.
   - If glare appears, move the phone or sheet slightly, or alter the indirect light angle; do not press, flatten, or otherwise alter the paper.
   - Recheck the corners and pale washes before shooting.

6. Capture
   - Take one full-sheet frame with all edges visible and minimal surrounding background.
   - Take three to five detail frames: the focal area, a light-to-dark transition, an edge or wash boundary, and any distinctive texture or small feature.
   - Keep the phone parallel for each detail and record which area each frame shows.

7. Finish
   - Review sharpness, complete edges, color consistency, and absence of glare before returning the sheet to storage.
   - Save the original files without editing; if making corrected copies, retain them separately and label them as derived.
   - Return the work to its normal protective storage promptly, out of direct light and with no fresh pressure on the paper.

This method section should not be approved as written. It allows repeated daily peeking, treats the first nominally significant result as sufficient for rollout, makes effect size optional, and removes the stabilization-cohort check. That is inconsistent with the experiment boundary: first statistical significance is not enough to ship.

Suggested replacement:

“Run the experiment through the predeclared complete weekly cohort window and preserve treatment and control assignments throughout that window. The primary conversion metric, analysis population, denominator, and decision threshold must be specified before launch. Daily monitoring may be used for delivery, assignment, instrumentation, support, unsubscribe, and other safety checks, but daily primary-metric results are descriptive and must not trigger rollout.

At the end of each complete weekly cohort, report the treatment and control denominators, absolute and relative effect sizes, uncertainty intervals, and p-value, together with assignment and delivery integrity and prespecified guardrails. Statistical significance alone is not sufficient for a product decision; the effect must also be decision-relevant and satisfy the guardrails.

Repeat the same predeclared analysis on the next complete weekly cohort and evaluate a separate stabilization cohort. Preserve first-cohort, subsequent-cohort, combined, and stabilization-cohort results separately. Rollout requires favorable evidence across the predeclared cohorts, including stabilization-cohort confirmation, acceptable support and unsubscribe guardrails, and no unresolved assignment, delivery, instrumentation, or semantic issue. If these conditions are not met, record the result as inconclusive or hold rollout rather than shipping on the first significant daily read.”

The phrase “Effect-size reporting is optional” should be removed entirely. Effect size, denominator, uncertainty, and decision relevance are required outputs, not optional interpretation.

Methodological conflicts

- The readout draws a conclusion before stating the observed effect size, denominator, or uncertainty.
- The primary metric and analysis window appear to be selected or interpreted after looking at the result rather than predeclared.
- Statistical significance is treated as sufficient evidence for rollout, without a decision-relevant effect threshold.
- The test window is not shown to be powered for the claimed effect or complete enough to support the conclusion.
- First significance is being conflated with durable evidence; no stabilization cohort is required before shipping.
- The framing risks debating the product hypothesis before establishing whether the measurement design supports the claim.

Concise revision comments

1. Please predeclare the primary metric, denominator, cohort definition, observation window, and decision-relevant effect threshold before interpreting the result.

2. Add the power basis for the stated window: target effect size, assumptions, required sample or exposure count, and whether the observed cohort completes that window.

3. Reorder the readout to show the denominator, observed effect size with uncertainty, and comparison against the decision threshold before any conclusion.

4. Do not treat first statistical significance as a rollout signal. Label it explicitly as first significance and keep rollout paused.

5. Add a stabilization-cohort requirement: repeat the same predeclared analysis on the next complete cohort, with the same metric, coding, window, and decision threshold, before a ship decision.

6. Keep this review methodological. First establish whether the metric, window, power, effect size, and replication support a decision; defer claims about the product hypothesis until those conditions are met.

Dry-flattening sequence

1. Wash and dry your hands. On a clean, dry, flat table, place a smooth rigid board larger than the 9 × 12-inch sheet.

2. Add clean archival interleaving—preferably smooth, unbuffered tissue or nonwoven polyester such as Hollytex. Avoid paper towels, newspaper, waxed paper, and anything textured or printed.

3. Place the sheet painted-side up on the interleaving. Do not rub, press, or test the paint surface.

4. Cover it with a second clean interleaf, then a second smooth rigid board larger than the sheet. The boards should contact only the interleaving, never the paint.

5. Add light, evenly distributed weight across the entire upper board—not concentrated on the curled edges. Begin with 30–60 minutes, then inspect by lifting the top board straight up.

6. If the sheet remains completely dry and unchanged, continue for several hours, checking periodically. Overnight is a reasonable maximum first attempt; extend only if there is clear improvement and no adverse sign.

Stop immediately and leave it alone if you see tackiness, pigment transfer, altered sheen, abrasion, pressure marks, edge catching, new cockling, or any moisture. If the curl is only modestly improved after the first overnight cycle, do not increase the weight; let the sheet rest flat and dry, then reassess later.

Conservative verification sequence

1. Freeze the state

   - Do not overwrite, rename, move, repair, resave, normalize, deduplicate, or synchronize either P027 copy.
   - Pause any sync, backup, photo-management, or indexing process that could rewrite metadata or replace a file.
   - Do not open either file in an editor that may write embedded metadata.
   - Keep the existing 40-file inventory and catalog unchanged.
   - If possible, work from read-only mounts, filesystem snapshots, or provider snapshots. If not, use read-only file access and record that the source volumes were not mounted read-only.

2. Create a separate incident record

   Record, without altering either source:

   - Local path and exact filename.
   - Cloud object path, object name, version/generation ID, or immutable object identifier.
   - The previously recorded cloud checksum, its algorithm, and where that value came from.
   - The date and time of this check, operator, tools, and tool versions.
   - File presence and readability for both copies.
   - The existing catalog statement: “April 1994 Portland garden outing; exact day unresolved.”
   - A neutral incident statement: “Local working copy does not match the stored checksum for the cloud object. No authority assigned based on this mismatch.”

   Keep this record separate from the image files and separate from the catalog’s date fields.

3. Capture local filesystem metadata

   Use read-only metadata inspection and save the output to a new evidence file, not into the source directory:

   ```sh
   stat -- "$LOCAL_P027"
   file -- "$LOCAL_P027"
   ```

   Record at least:

   - Byte size
   - Modification time
   - Change/status time
   - Birth/creation time if available
   - File mode and ownership
   - Filesystem/device and inode information if relevant

   These values describe the local filesystem copy. They do not establish preservation-master status.

4. Capture cloud object metadata without replacing the local file

   Use the cloud provider’s metadata or object-inspection function, not a sync or restore operation. Record:

   - Object size
   - Stored checksum and algorithm
   - Version/generation ID
   - Content type
   - Provider creation and modification times
   - User-defined metadata
   - Retention, immutability, legal-hold, or object-lock status
   - Audit history showing creation, replacement, deletion, or restoration events

   Do not treat an ETag as an MD5 or cryptographic checksum unless that provider explicitly documents that meaning for this object.

5. Hash the local copy

   If the cloud value is a SHA-256 checksum:

   ```sh
   sha256sum --binary -- "$LOCAL_P027"
   ```

   If the cloud uses another documented algorithm, calculate that same algorithm as well. Preserve the complete command output and tool version in the incident record.

   For an independent local calculation, a second implementation can be used without changing the file:

   ```sh
   openssl dgst -sha256 -- "$LOCAL_P027"
   ```

   Matching independent local calculations establish the local file’s hash consistently. They do not establish that the local file is the preservation master.

6. Compare the values exactly

   Compare:

   - Local byte size with the cloud object size.
   - Local calculated checksum with the cloud’s stored checksum.
   - The local checksum with any pre-existing locked manifest checksum for P027.
   - The cloud checksum with that same pre-existing manifest value.

   Do not “repair” a checksum record to make it match. Preserve the original value and record the comparison result as one of:

   - Local matches cloud.
   - Local does not match cloud.
   - Cloud checksum unavailable or algorithm unclear.
   - Manifest relationship unresolved.

7. Inspect embedded metadata read-only

   If metadata comparison is needed, extract it to a new report rather than writing it back:

   ```sh
   exiftool -G1 -a -s -j -- "$LOCAL_P027" > "$EVIDENCE_DIR/P027.local.exif.json"
   ```

   If a separately retrieved cloud copy is later available, run the same read-only extraction against that quarantine copy.

   Compare fields such as:

   - Embedded filename or image identifier
   - Capture or scan metadata
   - Scanner/software information
   - Resolution, dimensions, bit depth, compression, and color profile
   - Embedded modification fields
   - XMP/IPTC/EXIF/TIFF tags
   - Any sidecar references

   Embedded dates and filesystem dates are evidence about recorded metadata only. They must not be used to resolve the catalog’s exact day.

8. If content-level comparison is required, retrieve a new cloud copy into quarantine

   Do not restore over the local working copy. Download the cloud object to a newly created, non-synchronized quarantine location, preserving the provider’s version ID in the quarantine filename or log.

   Then:

   ```sh
   sha256sum --binary -- "$QUARANTINE_P027"
   cmp -- "$LOCAL_P027" "$QUARANTINE_P027"
   ```

   Verify the downloaded copy’s checksum against the cloud’s stored checksum before using it for comparison. A successful download is not proof that the download corresponds to the intended cloud version unless the version ID and checksum agree.

   The quarantine copy is an inspection copy, not automatically a new master.

9. Look for authority evidence, not merely matching bytes

   The strongest evidence that the cloud version is the preservation master would be a consistent chain such as:

   - A pre-existing preservation manifest identifies P027 and contains the same checksum as the cloud object.
   - The manifest is dated or versioned from the scan/ingest process and was retained independently of the cloud object.
   - The cloud object’s immutable version/generation ID corresponds to the object recorded in that manifest.
   - Cloud audit history shows creation from the preservation ingest and no unaccounted replacement.
   - An independent third copy, such as an external archive copy, matches the same checksum.
   - The scan log, operator notes, filename, photo ID, and provenance notes identify the same P027 item.
   - Any later access/viewing derivative is clearly distinguished from the preservation master.

   A checksum proves that two byte sequences are identical. It does not by itself prove which copy was created first, which was intended as the master, or which has the stronger chain of custody. Timestamps alone are insufficient.

10. Apply a fail-closed decision rule

   - Cloud matches the locked preservation manifest, immutable object identity, and an independent corroborating copy:
     designate that specific cloud version as the preservation master, subject to the archive’s documented authority rules. Keep the local mismatch unchanged as a non-authoritative working-copy exception.

   - Local matches the locked preservation manifest but cloud does not:
     do not designate either copy based only on the mismatch. Investigate whether the cloud object was replaced, corrupted, or associated with the wrong manifest/version. Preserve both unchanged.

   - Neither copy matches the locked manifest:
     status remains unresolved. Preserve both and escalate for provenance review; do not create a new “correct” master by preference.

   - No locked manifest or trustworthy chain-of-custody evidence exists:
     label the cloud copy and local copy with their observed hashes and evidence status, but do not claim that either is proven authoritative.

11. Preserve the date boundary

   Do not change the catalog date, add an exact day, or infer one from:

   - Filesystem timestamps
   - Embedded metadata
   - Cloud upload or modification time
   - Hash-verification time
   - The date of the mismatch discovery

   The catalog should continue to state only that P027 is linked to the April 1994 Portland garden outing, with the exact day unresolved. If an incident note is permitted, add only a separate verification note describing the checksum mismatch and evidence status; do not alter the date or provenance fields.

12. Final evidence package

   Retain, outside both source locations:

   - Original local and cloud checksum values
   - Newly calculated local checksum
   - Cloud object metadata and immutable version identifier
   - Local `stat` and `file` output
   - Read-only embedded-metadata reports
   - Any quarantine-download checksum and `cmp` result
   - Existing manifest and scan/provenance records
   - Cloud audit or retention evidence
   - The decision and unresolved questions
   - A statement that neither source was modified and that the catalog date remains unresolved

This sequence separates byte identity, metadata observation, chain-of-custody evidence, and catalog provenance, so the mismatch produces a controlled preservation exception rather than an unsupported correction.

1. Place the fully dry sheet level and mark a narrow dry buffer between the two passages.

2. Mix a transparent, pigment-rich dark with only enough water to move smoothly. Load the brush evenly; it should be wet, not dripping.

3. Paint the first passage in one controlled direction. Keep its bead small and moving—do not add water to chase it toward the second passage.

4. Check the approaching edge: if a bead thickens, blot the brush to barely damp and touch only the bead’s outer edge once. Lift; do not scrub or back-brush.

5. Stop before the passage reaches the dry buffer. Leave the buffer visibly dry and let the first passage dry undisturbed.

6. Test dryness by looking across the surface: no sheen, no darker pooled edge, and no cool-looking damp area. A light fingertip check on an unpainted margin can confirm that the sheet itself is no longer cool or soft.

7. Paint the second passage from its opposite side toward the buffer, using the same restrained load. Keep its wet edge inside its half of the gap.

8. Let the second passage dry completely before making any adjustment. If either edge is too hard, soften only with a nearly dry, clean brush placed once along the dry edge—not by rewetting both passages.

Stop immediately if the buffer begins to glisten, either bead starts flowing sideways, or the brush begins lifting pigment.

1. Test first: On a scrap of the same paper, try the diluted transparent cool neutral—blue-violet or blue-gray, not orange or a strongly complementary mix. Let it dry and choose a value that cools the shadow without making it markedly darker.

2. Protect the edge: Leave a narrow dry strip of warm wood visible. Do not carry the glaze up to that strip; preserve the warmth by keeping the cool glaze separated by value, not by adding saturation.

3. Control moisture: Load a clean soft brush with the thin glaze, then blot once until it is damp and controlled rather than wet. The brush should release color without flooding the paper.

4. Apply once: Start in the middle of the shadow mass and move outward in one connected pass. Keep the warm-edge strip untouched. Use progressively lighter pressure and a less-loaded brush toward the far side.

5. Plan the stop: End inside the shadow at a preselected, slightly irregular edge—not at the warm wood boundary. Taper the final stroke to nearly dry, lift, and leave it. Do not chase a drying line with a clean wet brush.

6. Stop completely: No scrubbing, re-entry, or added orange saturation. Let the sheet dry fully, then judge the cooled shadow and retained warm edge only after drying.

1. Make a small value test on the same paper: compare the existing shadow with one dilute blue-violet or blue-gray glaze. Choose the mix that deepens value modestly without noticeably increasing saturation.

2. Mark two zones: a short “lost” section and a separate “found” section. Keep the found section completely dry and protected.

3. With a clean, damp—not wet—brush, rewet only the shadow side, stopping just beside the pale ceramic edge. Do not place water on or over the pale edge.

4. Starting in the shadow’s middle, make one connected glaze pass toward the lost section. Feather inward on the shadow side with a nearly dry brush, ending in a slightly irregular, soft transition. Let the pale edge remain untouched so it recedes optically into the darkening shadow.

5. Leave the found section dry, then place a controlled, slightly stronger pass right up to its boundary with a clean, deliberate stroke. Keep that section narrow and crisp.

6. Stop. Do not scrub, lift, chase drying lines, or warm the mixture with more orange.

7. Let the paper dry completely before judging the lost-versus-found effect.Wetness can make the transition look softer and darker than it will be when dry.

Date/time reported: September 4, 2027, 10:25 a.m. Central

The kitchen faucet has developed a steady drip from the spout when both handles are fully off. The shutoff valves and supply lines beneath the sink are dry. There is no cabinet swelling, water intrusion, electrical hazard, drainage problem, or loss of water service.

Please treat the following as urgent and advise us how to proceed if any occur:

- Dripping becomes a continuous flow or increases substantially.
- Water appears beneath the sink, at a shutoff valve, or along a supply line.
- Water reaches the cabinet floor, walls, or nearby electrical components.
- Cabinet swelling, pooling, staining, or other water damage appears.
- A handle becomes loose, stuck, difficult to operate, or cannot shut off the water.
- The faucet body, connections, or sprayer begins leaking.

1. Make three small swatches on the same cold-press paper, all with the same brush:
   - A: 1 part yellow ochre pigment to about 3 parts water.
   - B: 1 part pigment to 5 parts water.
   - C: 1 part pigment to 7 parts water.
   Use only yellow ochre—do not add orange, sienna, or another warm pigment.

2. Apply each with a soft, moderately loaded brush: charge it, then touch it once to the palette edge so it is damp and carrying color, not dripping. Lay one connected stroke without scrubbing or returning to the drying edge.

3. Test board angles of flat and about 10°. For the wall passage, begin at roughly a 10° incline, with the passage’s upper edge slightly higher. Keep the wash moving gently; if a bead forms at the lower edge, wick only that bead with the clean, nearly dry brush tip.

4. Let the swatches dry completely. Choose the palest ratio that still reads as a wall—probably B or C—and the angle with the least dark pigment lodged in the texture.

5. On the dry sheet, use that same diluted mix and brush load. Work one quiet, continuous pass at the selected slight incline, then stop. Do not soften, lift, or re-enter it while drying; judge the sedimentation only after it is fully dry.

Best default: leave it for now and view the study at arm’s length or in a photograph. If the line disappears into the quiet margin, it may be harmless and erasing could create more disturbance than the graphite.

If it remains distracting:

1. Place the sheet on a firm, clean surface.
2. Use a clean, soft kneaded eraser—not a vinyl eraser.
3. Dab or gently lift along the graphite; do not scrub or make repeated passes.
4. Keep the eraser confined to the margin and remove crumbs by tilting or using a soft brush, not by rubbing.
5. Stop immediately if the paper develops a lighter patch, sheen, roughness, or pigment transfer.

Do not dampen or lift the area. Given the location and condition, one restrained kneaded-eraser pass is reasonable, but preserving the quiet margin untouched remains the safest choice.

1. Let the sheet dry completely. View the line at normal viewing distance and at arm’s length, then squint. If it does not materially distract from the painting, leave it.

2. If removal is warranted, test only a tiny end of the line with a clean kneaded eraser. Roll or lift lightly; do not rub, scrub, wet, or use a hard eraser.

3. Inspect immediately. If the line lightens cleanly and the paper’s texture and sheen remain unchanged, make one similarly light pass along the remainder.

4. Stop at once if the cold-press tooth resists, the line does not release promptly, fibers lift, the surface abrades, pigment moves, or the sheen changes. Leave the remaining line rather than escalating pressure.

Test and application sequence

1. Mix enough paint for the entire passage, plus a small reserve. Use the ultramarine-and-burnt-sienna mixture already matched to the pale value; add water to lighten it, not extra burnt sienna. Mix thoroughly until no warmer streaks remain.

2. On the dry cold-press strip, mark the passage lightly. Set the board at a modest angle, about 15–20°, so the wash moves gently but does not run.

3. Load the brush fully but evenly. Touch it once to a towel only if it is dripping; do not work with a thirsty brush. The point should remain charged throughout the passage.

4. Start at the upper edge. Lay the first stroke, then move steadily across or downward, overlapping each stroke while the previous edge is still uniformly wet. Keep the brush moving in one connected passage.

5. Do not return to correct streaks, scrub the texture, lift paint, or chase drying edges. Stop at the planned boundary and leave the wash alone to dry completely.

6. If the orange becomes stronger, the brush is probably concentrating the sienna during re-entry or uneven loading. Remix the reserve to the original pale neutral mixture; do not add more sienna to the paper. Judge the result only after full drying.
